newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba's Meister warns Bonn not to risk credibility.
newsitem.headline: Buba's Meister warns Bonn not to risk credibility.

text.p: Bundesbank board member Edgar Meister said on Monday Bonn's efforts to cover an 18 billion mark tax revenue shortfall will be closely scrutinised and warned the government not to gamble with its credibility.

Meister's remarks follow the announcement of a controversial plan by Finance Minister Theo Waigel to revalue the central bank's gold and currency reserves in a bid to qualify for the planned single European currency.

The revaluation, aimed at cutting the public debt and deficit, has been widely denounced as hypocrisy in Germany and in some European countries, where memories linger of Waigel's stern warnings against creative accounting to meet the Maastricht Treaty's strict convergence criteria.

"The results of the most recent tax estimate show how 'thorny' qualification for the single European currency is for Germany as well," Meister said according to the text of a speech to be held in Buenos Aires.
"One will now watch very closely to see with what measures the financing deficit will be countered."
Meister added: "It is decisive...to achieve sustainable convergence if politicians do not want to gamble with their credibility in the markets and among the public."
But costs resulting from German unification in 1990 must not be completely ignored in assessing Germany's level of public debt, he said.
The Bundesbank made a text of the speech to the Argentine banking association ADEBA available ahead of delivery.
Meister made no specific reference to Waigel's gold revaluation plans in the text of the speech.

The bank has so far declined comment on the plan beyond a brief statement saying Waigel had presented it with initial proposals for changes to Bundesbank accounting methods relating to the transfer of responsibilities to the European central bank (ECB).

But the central bank is believed to be concerned at the direct link between the revaluation of reserves -- necessary in any case as part of the transfer of reserves to the ECB -- and the government's budget problems.

"Measures which only have a short-term effect to window dress the financial situation, or even pure accounting tricks which shift part of the deficit into the future do not only lead to a loss of confidence on financial markets and among the public," Meister said.
"They would also become transparent soon after the start of monetary union."

Waigel, faced with the tax revenue shortfall, has said that if central bank reserves were revalued from current low book prices to levels closer to the normal market price it could help close the gap.
A revaluation would effectively deliver Bonn a windfall profit, allowing it to retire billions in old debt.
Meister warned that the time pressure on governments to qualify for the planned launch on January 1, 1999 must not lead to a less stability-oriented interpretation of the criteria.

"Even if markets have today already firmly factored in a punctual start of monetary union, as shown in convergence trading, and even if politicians keep confirming these expectations, the stability-oriented adherence to the criteria is not yet assured for Germany either," Meister said.
A strict interpretation of the convergence criteria and lasting adherence to them were a "central precondition" for the stability of the monetary union.

Germany has been strongly against any kind of budget fudges for European economic and monetary union, but record unemployment, which may average 4.3 million in 1997, has left Bonn struggling to meet the entry criteria.
The Maastricht Treaty says countries joining EMU should aim to have budget deficits no higher than 3 percent of gross domestic product and overall debts not more than 60 percent of GDP.

Germany failed to meet both those criteria in 1996 and despite Bonn's continued insistence that it will qualify for the Euro in time, independent economists expect it to overshoot both levels again in 1997, the key year for judging which nations can join.
